title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm P\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm P\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.
why: Semidefinite constraints underlie many successful optimization relaxations, yet their unrestricted exact decision complexity is still unsettled. This problem isolates whether finite rational input admits a polynomial-time decision even when numerical separation and small explicit witnesses are unavailable.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

progress.text: Ramana establishes exact alternatives and the distinction between simultaneous NP/coNP membership in the Turing model and membership in both real-machine classes.
De Klerk–Vallentin analyze polynomial bit complexity of short-step interior-point approximation under supplied geometric assumptions.
The expanded symbolic-degeneracy paper specifies generic objectives/auxiliary choices and arithmetic-complexity qualifications.

Pataki’s current duality preprint retains the unrestricted feasibility complexity question.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The October/November 2025 primary texts and the September 2026 higher-order Newton paper explicitly retain the unknown exact SDP complexity. Current exact-duality, restricted approximation and symbolic results do not establish polynomial bit-time decision for all rational inputs. No verified full resolution was found in bounded searches. The card remains source_open; this pass does not independently certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A semidefinite constraint requires a quadratic form to be nonnegative in every direction. Diagonal matrix inequalities include ordinary linear inequalities. Exact decision asks whether the feasible region is empty, which is different from obtaining a useful approximate optimizer on well-conditioned instances.

De Klerk–Vallentin’s inspected approximation theorem is supplied with a rational feasible center and quantitative inner and outer radius information. Its runtime also depends on requested accuracy. This is a polynomial bit-complexity result under explicit geometric assumptions, not an unrestricted exact emptiness test.

Approximate feasibility need not imply exact feasibility. For example,
\[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\]
has determinant \(-1\), so it is never positive semidefinite. Nevertheless its negative eigenvalue \((t-\sqrt{t^2+4})/2\) tends to zero as \(t\) tends to positive infinity. This infeasible affine family has distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone in the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of squared matrix entries.

A rational input can also have only irrational feasible parameters. The rational affine block-diagonal matrix
\[\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\2&2x\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}2&x\\x&1\end{pmatrix}\right)\]
is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x=\sqrt2\). Replacing the real domain by rational substitutions would change the answer to this instance.

Even when rational feasible points exist, all of them can require exponentially many bits relative to the number of variables. Pataki–Touzov study the structural occurrence of such examples and questions about compact representations. This explains an obstacle to algorithms that must explicitly output a point; it does not itself lower-bound the complexity of the decision bit requested here.

General exact decision is possible through real-algebraic methods. Henrion–Naldi–Safey El Din develop symbolic algorithms accommodating degenerate feasible sets. Their optimization analysis retains generic auxiliary choices and objectives, and its displayed bounds count arithmetic operations. Bounds polynomial when one dimension is fixed do not establish one polynomial bit bound when both dimensions and coefficient lengths vary.

Ramana’s exact alternative replaces infeasibility by feasibility of another semidefinite system of polynomial description size. In the Turing model it implies that the problem lies in NP if and only if it lies in coNP; neither membership is thereby established on its own. The separate NP-intersect-coNP result over exact real-number machines uses a different model of computation.

Pataki’s October 2025 treatment retains this complexity distinction and gives a fuller description of the exact dual’s feasible set. A polynomial-size dual system is not automatically a polynomial-size binary certificate: its real variables still have to satisfy semidefinite constraints.

Slot–Steurer–Wiedmer obtain effective solution bounds and polynomial-time approximate minimization of convex polynomials over polyhedra. The constraints in that result are linear, and the authors explicitly contrast their result with general semidefinite programming. It does not make arbitrary linear matrix inequalities decidable in polynomial bit time.

The September 2026 higher-order Newton paper of ter Voert–de Klerk explicitly retains the unknown exact SDP complexity. Its iteration analysis uses a derivative oracle and real-number computation, and fixed-accuracy SDP subproblems require stated regularity. A reduction of an iteration to an SDP is therefore not a solution of this unrestricted Turing-model decision question.

The target is a deterministic polynomial bit-time decision of whether some real substitution makes the matrix positive semidefinite.
Singular feasible points, irrational-only feasible parameters, unbounded sets and infeasible instances at zero distance from the cone are included.
Known approximation and exact-duality results retain assumptions or model distinctions, and the September 2026 source still states the unrestricted exact complexity as open.
A complete Lean proof must establish one polynomial-time decider or exclude all such deciders; it need not output a feasible point or optimization value.

source_formulation.text: The retained target is unrestricted rational-data semidefinite feasibility in the ordinary bit model, as discussed by Ramana, Pataki–Touzov and the later duality literature. This card chooses the equivalent affine linear-matrix-inequality representation and explicitly makes the variables real. It asks for a decision bit, without adding an optimization or witness-output task. The zero-variable case fixes the harmless endpoint of the input domain.
